title: The fast I have chosen (Isaiah 58:6–7)
hookLine: read on Yom Kippur: loose the bonds, share your bread, house the poor

lines: YOM KIPPUR MORNING. NO FOOD, NO WATER.
IS THIS THE FAST I WANT?
cards: It's the morning of Yom Kippur. The synagogue is full of people who haven't eaten since the evening before. No food, no water, hours of prayer.
And in the middle of it, someone stands up to read from the prophets, and the reading is Isaiah fifty-eight, in which God asks, more or less: is this the fast I want?
On the fast day itself, the fasting people hear a prophet question their fasting. Some readers think that placement is the whole point.

teach.b: The chapter starts with the people's complaint: "Wherefore have we fasted, say they, and thou seest not?" We did everything right; why isn't God noticing?
The prophet answers: on the day of your fast you still chase your own business and push your workers hard. You fast and quarrel.

Then comes the turn: "Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke? Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house? when thou seest the naked, that thou cover him; and that thou hide not thyself from thine own flesh?"
What the prophet does not say matters.
He doesn't say: stop fasting. Yom Kippur is still a fast, and the people hearing this chapter are still hungry. He says the fast was never only about the empty stomach.
It points somewhere: to the person whose stomach is empty without choosing it.

teach.h: HIDE NOT THYSELF FROM THINE OWN FLESH.
teach.b: And that last phrase: hide not thyself from thine own flesh. Don't look away from another human being, as if they weren't your own family.

teach.h: DEAL THY BREAD TO THE HUNGRY.
teach.b: Going hungry for a day, the chapter suggests, is meant to make a person notice the people who are hungry every day.

how: Isaiah 58 is read as the prophetic reading on Yom Kippur morning, and some Jews mark the day by giving charity or bringing food for those in need as the fast ends.

o: a feast held at the close of a holiday
a prayer said on behalf of the hungry
a fast, a day without food, like Yom Kippur

games.q: the fast I have chosen — tap the pairs.

s: Isaiah 58 tells people to stop fasting
it says the fast was never only about the empty stomach, and Yom Kippur is still a fast.
the chapter is read on Yom Kippur, while people are fasting
the fasting people hear a prophet question their fasting.
in the chapter, the people think God is pleased
they complain: wherefore have we fasted, and thou seest not?

games.q: you've fasted all day. you ask God why it seems to make no difference. what does the prophet tell you the chosen fast is?
o: freeing the oppressed and sharing your bread.
games.why: "is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry?" the fast points outward, to the people who are hungry without choosing it.

practice: Notice your own stomach for a moment, full, empty or somewhere in between, then let your mind go outward to who near you might be hungry today: a neighbor, a shelter, a coworker who skips lunch.
Hold them in mind, and if you pray, hold the verse: is not this the fast that I have chosen?
